name: Zambian Ifisashi
description: Ifisashi, leafy greens cooked into a real groundnut sauce, is one of Zambia's most cherished everyday dishes - its name literally translates to 'groundnut sauce' in Bemba. Real technique roasts raw groundnuts and grinds them fresh into a powder, rather than using commercial peanut butter directly, then builds a proper tomato-onion base before the greens go in.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

ingredients_full.note: standing in for pumpkin or sweet potato leaves

ingredients.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

ingredients.note: standing in for pumpkin or sweet potato leaves

steps_detailed: Cook the onion and garlic in a little oil, 4-5 minutes, until softened.
Add the tomatoes and cook until it forms a thick paste, 5-6 minutes.
Stir in the ground peanuts to coat, then add the spinach and a splash of water.
Cover and simmer 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the greens are tender and the sauce has thickened.

name: Zambian Nshima
description: Nshima, a stiff maize porridge, is Zambia's most essential staple starch, eaten daily by hand alongside ifisashi and other stews.
steps_detailed: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.
Gradually beat in the remaining cornmeal, stirring vigorously, over medium-low heat 15-18 minutes, until very thick and it pulls away from the sides of the pot.

name: Zambian Village Chicken Stew
description: Free-range village chicken stewed simply with tomato and onion, real Zambian versions letting the chicken simmer long and slow since village-raised birds are naturally tougher and more flavorful than commercial chicken.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion and garlic, 8-9 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and a splash of water, and simmer 30-35 minutes, longer than a quick-cooking bird would need, until deeply tender.

name: Zambian T-Bone Steak
description: Grilled T-bone steak is a genuine point of pride in Zambian cuisine, reflecting the country's real cattle-ranching tradition, real technique letting the steak rest after grilling so the juices redistribute.
steps_detailed: Rub the steak with the garlic and oil.
Grill over high heat, 4-5 minutes per side for medium, until well charred.
Rest 5 minutes before slicing, so the juices redistribute rather than spilling out.
steps: Rub the steak with the garlic and oil.

name: Zambian Kapenta Stew
description: Kapenta, small dried freshwater fish, is a genuine Zambian staple protein from Lake Kariba and Lake Tanganyika - canned sardines stand in here as the closest widely available small dried-fish substitute.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Fish, sardine, Atlantic, canned in oil, drained solids with bone

name: Zambian Ibwabwa (Pumpkin Leaves)
description: Chibwabwa, pumpkin leaves cooked simply with groundnuts, one of the most common real ifisashi variations, real technique adding a little baking soda to help soften the leaves faster.

Stir in the ground peanuts and simmer 10 minutes more until thickened.

name: Zambian Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish rubbed with garlic and lemon, reflecting Zambia's freshwater fishing tradition along the Zambezi River.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and lemon juice, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.

name: Zambian Sweet Potato Fritters
description: Simple fried sweet potato fritters, a common Zambian snack, real technique squeezing excess moisture from the grated sweet potato first.
steps_detailed: Squeeze the grated sweet potato well to remove excess moisture, then mix with the flour.
Fry spoonfuls, turning, 3-4 minutes, until golden and cooked through.

name: Zambian Beef and Vegetable Stew
description: A simple, hearty beef and vegetable stew, common Zambian home cooking, real technique browning the beef properly first to build real flavor.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion, 8-9 minutes.
Add the carrot, potato, and tomatoes, and simmer 30-35 minutes until tender.

name: Zambian Fried Cassava
description: Simple fried cassava, a common Zambian side dish, real technique parboiling first so it crisps outside while staying tender inside.
steps_detailed: Boil the cassava until just tender, 12-15 minutes.
Fry in the oil, turning, 5-6 minutes, until golden and crisp outside.
Season with salt while still hot.

name: Zambian Fried Plantain
description: Fried ripe plantain, a common Zambian side dish, real versions using genuinely ripe plantain for real caramelization.
steps_detailed: Fry the plantain slices in the oil, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized and golden.

name: Zambian Coleslaw
description: A mayonnaise-dressed cabbage salad, a common Zambian side, real versions with a touch of mustard for depth.
steps_detailed: Whisk the mayonnaise and mustard together.
Toss with the cabbage and carrot until well coated.

description: A simple tomato and onion salad, a common Zambian side, real technique letting the onion sit briefly in lemon juice first.
steps_detailed: Toss the onion with the lemon juice and let sit 5 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and toss together.

name: Zambian Milk Tea
description: Sweetened milk tea is a beloved daily ritual across Zambia, real versions simmering the tea and milk together rather than just steeping.
steps_detailed: Warm the tea and milk together 5 minutes.
Stir in the sugar before serving.

description: A simple roasted sweet potato side, a common Zambian staple.
